pageTitle: ffl — Transfer for humans and agents
pageDescription: Turn a file, folder, or stream into a link. A person opens it in a browser; an agent fetches it with the CLI or MCP. Native TCP/QUIC P2P, WebRTC, and relay fallback. No cloud-storage upload required.
socialDescription: One link. A person opens it in a browser, an agent fetches it and keeps working. The bytes go from your machine to theirs.
heroDesc: Turn a file, folder, or stream into a link. A person opens it in a browser. An agent fetches it and keeps working. The bytes go from your machine to theirs, not through a cloud bucket.
heroNote: Free direct sharing. No account. Apache-2.0 core.
filmLabel: Film: how one ffl link reaches a person and an agent
cap1: Most file handoffs take a detour through somebody's cloud.
cap2: ffl turns your folder into a link. The files stay on your machine.
cap3: A person opens the link in a browser. Nothing to install.
cap4: An agent fetches the same link and carries on with its job.
cap5: Direct when possible, relay when needed. With --e2ee, the relay only carries ciphertext.
cap6: Checksum verified on arrival. One link, any next step.
handoffTitle: One command. Any kind of recipient.
handoffDesc: A photo album, a build artifact, a model checkpoint. The sender runs the same command; what changes is who picks it up.
humanNote: No recipient account or app. Keep the sender running until the download finishes.
agentNote: Read the link from handoff.json and pass it through your orchestrator. Events stream to events.jsonl. Keep the sender alive until delivery completes.
lanNote: No public tunnel. LAN links use HTTP, so use a trusted network and --e2ee for file contents. The tunnel choice is remembered; restore internet sharing with --preferred-tunnel default.
copyFailed: Clipboard unavailable. The command is selected; copy it with your keyboard.
watchDesc: With --watch, every new child folder is published once it stops changing. The receiver runs --follow on one collection link and picks up each batch as it lands.
watchNote: New folders only. Append-only delivery, not a mirror or two-way sync.
watchLink: Read the watch and follow guide
routesTitle: Your bytes take the shortest route you allow.
routesDesc: Cloud storage shouldn't be a prerequisite for handing over a file. ffl connects sender and receiver directly, and you choose how it reaches the network.
routeInternetNote: ffl clients connect over native TCP/QUIC; browsers use WebRTC. Public signaling and tunnel services help the two sides find each other, and an HTTPS relay carries the transfer when a direct connection fails.
routeLocalNote: Explicit LAN mode binds to a local IP and skips public tunnels. Both devices must reach that address, and the listening port must be allowed through the firewall.
privacyInternet: Add --e2ee to encrypt file contents on both the direct and relay paths. Connection metadata stays visible. Prefer your own infrastructure? Use Cloudflare, ngrok, a self-hosted sish tunnel, or Tor.
privacyLocal: LAN links use HTTP. --e2ee encrypts file contents, but the page and metadata are not. Use a trusted network.
courierTitle: Make sure it reaches the right hands.
courierDesc: A link is easy to forward. When that matters, ask the recipient to prove who they are before the download starts.
pickupDesc: The recipient enters a 6-digit code before downloading. ffl generates one if you don't set it.
pubkeyDesc: Only the holder of the matching private key can open the download. Create keys with ffl keygen.
checksumDesc: Every download is verified on the receiving side, in the browser or the CLI, so a corrupted file never passes silently.
receiptDesc: Get an email when the download finishes, or ask the receiver to confirm. Requires an eligible account.
agentsTitle: Your agents make things. Give them a way to deliver.
agentsDesc: Move a local model, a dataset, or a generated report between machines without a cloud bucket or a shared filesystem. Your orchestrator passes the link; ffl carries the bytes.
cliDesc: Share files or stdin. Read the link from --json, follow progress with --hook, close after one download with --max-downloads 1, stream to another program with --stdout.
mcpTitle: As a tool for your agent
mcpDesc: Connect the companion ffl-mcp server to any MCP host. Agents can share outputs and download inputs, then hand the same link to a person.
embedDesc: Structured events and host-provided file sources let you build transfers into your product. Your app owns the interface; ffl handles delivery.
installTitle: Install on the sender. The recipient just opens the link.
installUnixNote: Native builds for Linux x86_64 and macOS (Intel and Apple Silicon). On Linux ARM64, use the portable build.
installWindowsNote: Native Windows x86_64. The script downloads the official release and adds ffl to your PATH.
installApeNote: One portable executable for Windows, Linux, and macOS, including ARM64. Run it as ./ffl.com.
faq1Q: Is there a file-size limit or a cloud quota?
faq1A: Direct sharing has no cloud-storage quota and needs no account. The real limits are your network, your disk, and how long the sender stays online. Relay providers may set their own limits. Optional server upload has separate account and plan limits.
faq2Q: Does the sender need to stay online?
faq2A: Yes, for direct and relayed sharing. Keep ffl running and the files in place until the receiver finishes. If both sides can't be online together, --upload stores the file on a server for a while; that needs an account and the Upload addon.
faq3A: No, it's opt-in. Add --e2ee to encrypt file contents on direct and relay paths, then receive with ffl or its browser page. Metadata stays visible, and E2EE alone doesn't stop an active man-in-the-middle; use pickup codes or public keys to verify the recipient.
faq4Q: Is ffl an agent framework or a sync drive?
faq4A: Neither. ffl is the transfer layer. Your agent host or orchestrator decides what to send, passes the link, and manages processes. --watch publishes new child folders once they settle; it doesn't mirror edits or deletions.
footerTagline: From your machine to whatever comes next.
